summary: Defines a user-based security model for the SNMPv2 administrative framework, intended to provide authentication and privacy for management messages. It was experimental and is now historic.

eli5.summary: A guard at the door who checks that each person is who they say, and that nobody listens in. This described how such a guard would work for network management messages.

questions: what is the user-based security model for snmpv2
how does snmpv2 user-based security work
what authentication and encryption does usm use
how does usm protect against replay attacks
subtitle: Security model for SNMPv2 using user identity, authentication, and encryption.

tldr.problem: SNMPv2 needed a security model to protect management messages from modification, masquerade, replay attacks, and eavesdropping while remaining practical for network management in stressed conditions.
tldr.mechanism: The User-based Security Model (USM) identifies management operations by a named user, authenticates messages using MD5 digest and shared secrets, defends against replay using agent boot counts and timestamps, and encrypts sensitive data using DES in CBC mode.
tldr.outcome: USM provided the first security model for SNMPv2's administrative framework. It is now historic, superseded by more modern approaches. Time synchronization between managers and agents is required for authenticated communication.

facts.label: Privacy Key Size
facts.value: 16 octets (8 for DES key, 8 for IV)

today: RFC 1910 is experimental and historic. SNMPv2 security was later superseded by SNMPv3, which introduced the User-based Security Model in RFC 3414 with more robust algorithms and mechanisms. USM design influenced SNMPv3 security but is no longer used in practice.

sections.title: Introduction to SNMPv2 Security
sections.content:
Network management involves a management station sending commands to agents running on network devices like routers and switches. The SNMPv2 administrative framework defines mechanisms for authentication, authorization, access control, and privacy. A security model specifies the mechanisms used to achieve a given level of security for protocol interactions.

The User-based Security Model for SNMPv2 (USM) is the first and primary security model for SNMPv2. It identifies management operations by a user (named entity) on whose behalf a message is generated, enabling access control policies based on user identity. The RFC identifies four principal threats: modification of management information, masquerade as an authorized user, message stream modification (reordering or replay), and eavesdropping on management exchanges.
sections.eli5: Network managers use SNMP to monitor and control devices. USM protects those messages by proving who is sending them, making sure they have not been changed, detecting old replayed messages, and scrambling them so nobody listens in.

sections.title: Security Services and Mechanisms
sections.content:
USM provides three security services: data integrity (data has not been altered), data origin authentication (the claimed user identity is verified), and data confidentiality (information is not disclosed to unauthorized parties). The model uses MD5 message digest for authentication, with a 128-bit digest carried in each message. A shared secret known only to authorized entities is inserted into and appended to the message before digest computation, making verification of the digest equivalent to verifying the user identity.

Against replay attacks, each message includes agentID (unique agent identifier), agentBoots (reboot counter), and agentTime (seconds since last reboot), plus a request-id for responses. Managers validate that received messages have recent timestamps (within a 150-second window) and that responses match outstanding requests. For confidentiality, the model uses Data Encryption Standard (DES) in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, encrypting the PDU portion of messages with a 16-octet privacy key (8-octet DES key plus 8-octet initialization vector).
sections.eli5: USM uses three tricks: a signature made from a secret so only the real user can make it, a timestamp and boot counter so old messages are rejected, and scrambling with DES so the actual command stays hidden.

sections.title: Elements of the Security Model
sections.content:
Each SNMPv2 user has four attributes: userName (octet string identifier), authProtocol (indication of authentication capability and method), authPrivateKey (secret key for authentication), privProtocol (indication of privacy capability), and privPrivateKey (secret key for encryption).

Messages are generated with a Quality of Service (QoS) that indicates whether authentication and privacy are used: no authentication and privacy, authentication only, or both authentication and privacy. The model also supports contexts (collections of management information accessible by an agent). Contexts can be local (directly realized) or proxy (forwarded to another agent). An SNMPv2 agent maintains agentBoots and agentTime in non-volatile storage to survive reboots. Managers must achieve and maintain time synchronization with agents by keeping local copies of agentBoots, agentTime, and latestReceivedAgentTime. Access policy determines which operations a user may perform on which objects in which contexts.
sections.eli5: Each user has a name and two secret passwords: one for proving their identity and one for scrambling messages. Messages say whether they use one password, both, or neither. Agents keep track of boot count and time to catch replay attacks. Managers synchronize their clock with the agent so they can check if a message is new or old.

sections.title: Message Format and Structure
sections.content:
An SNMPv2 message using USM contains a version field (set to 2), an administrative parameters field (OCTET STRING), and a data field (either plaintext PDU or encrypted OCTET STRING). The parameters field concatenates administrative data in network-byte order: 8-bit QoS, 12-octet agentID, 32-bit agentBoots, 32-bit agentTime, 16-bit maxSize (maximum message size the sender can receive), 1-octet user name length, 1 to 16 octet user name, 1-octet authentication digest length, 0 to 255 octet authentication digest (or empty for unauthenticated messages), and 0 to 40 octet context selector.

When authentication is used, the digest is computed over the entire message after encryption (if privacy is used). When privacy is used, only the PDU portion is encrypted using DES-CBC. The RFC specifies that multiple users may be defined at multiple agents, and each manager must have knowledge of each user and its attributes at each agent it manages.
sections.eli5: Each message is a package with the version number, a bunch of control information (who, what time, how big, what kind of security), and either the actual command in plain sight or scrambled.

sections.title: Message Generation and Processing
sections.content: When generating a request or notification, an SNMPv2 entity selects the appropriate user, authentication and privacy settings, and QoS, then computes the authentication digest (if authentication is enabled) and encrypts the PDU (if privacy is enabled). For received communication, the entity parses the message, checks the QoS, validates the authentication digest, verifies that the message's time is within the agent's time window, checks that the sender is the intended recipient (for agents), ensures the request-id matches outstanding requests (for managers), and increments error counters for any problems. If an agent receives an invalid authenticated message and the QoS indicates a report may be generated, the agent sends a report PDU containing error information. Managers use authenticated responses and Inform requests from agents to advance their local time synchronization and ensure they are aware of agent reboots. The model allows for discovery, where a manager can learn an agent's agentID and establish initial synchronization by sending an unencrypted request and examining error reports.
sections.eli5: When sending, the sender signs the message with a secret signature and maybe scrambles it. When receiving, the receiver checks that the signature is real, the message is new (not an old replay), and it matches what was expected, then acts on it or sends back an error.
